study.question: Does cross-action pooling fail because it overwrites already available same-action temporal comparisons, rather than because all additional support is unhelpful? Baseline AUC static0.6050036145, pooled0.6102261137, DIN0.6133619861 establishes usable histories. Latest matched cells: same_rank0.62005987699, pooled_rank0.61969186701, same_presence0.61988625211, pooled_presence0.61984483402. Thus pooling loses0.00036801 for rank while its presence-only loss is0.00004142. On the candidate-supplied first512 diagnostic impressions, pooling expands coordinate support0.15576171875 to0.305419921875 and changes existing ranks by mean0.05933291465. This confounds coverage and common-support value changes; neither mechanism has been isolated. Diagnostics are not population frequencies.
study.hypothesis: A deterministic fallback can preserve action-specific temporal evidence while borrowing a pooled-action anchor only when the same-action anchor is missing. If overwriting common-support ranks is harmful but some added ranks are informative, fallback should outperform full pooling and the no-extension control. This is provisional; pooling may instead add noise, suppress useful duplicate-rank optimization, or merely interact with one initialization.

study.proposed_difference: Let S denote required same-action support, P pooled support (S subset P), r the same-action gated rank, and p pooled gated rank. The unchanged main input is r. The four auxiliary inputs before fixed gain0.5 are: same_only=r; fallback_rank=where(S,r,p); common_pooled=S*p; pooled_all=p. All summaries are computed in every variant, replacing only existing auxiliary columns with no capacity/RNG changes. Fallback is conditional borrowing by support, unlike unconditional pooling or all-anchor averaging. Global novelty is unverified; no primary search hit establishes absence of nearest prior work.
